analysis.one_liner: Lets pharmacies, wholesalers, and individuals import lower-priced prescription drugs from peer countries.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in June 2024 and never received a hearing or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the Health and Human Services Department, within a year, to write rules letting American wholesale distributors, pharmacies, and individuals import qualifying prescription drugs from Canada, the United Kingdom, European Union members, and Switzerland — countries where the same drugs routinely sell for far less than in the United States. Individuals could import up to a 90-day personal supply from certified foreign pharmacies with a valid prescription. It also makes it illegal for drugmakers to charge foreign sellers higher prices than domestic customers in those countries, or to cut off or delay supplies to keep imports from competing with higher U.S. prices. The bill was introduced in June 2024, referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and died there when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who skip or ration prescriptions because of cost — the bill's findings cite tens of millions who have declined to fill a prescription due to price. It would let patients buy the same medicines from certified pharmacies in countries where prices are a fraction of U.S. prices, and let pharmacies and wholesalers import in bulk, which could lower prices for people with insurance too. People who already import medicines at personal legal risk, sometimes having shipments seized at the border, would get a legal channel with certified sellers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Americans who skip prescriptions over cost

how_it_helps.text: The bill cites findings that U.S. prescription drug prices average 2.78 times the price in comparable OECD countries, and 4.22 times for patented drugs, and that tens of millions of Americans have skipped filling a prescription because of cost. [S2]

Within one year of enactment, the Secretary of Health and Human Services must issue regulations allowing wholesale distributors and pharmacies to import qualifying drugs from Canada, the UK, EU member states, and Switzerland, and individuals to import up to a 90-day personal supply from certified foreign pharmacies with a valid prescription. [S2]

The bill requires a public list of certified foreign sellers, random laboratory testing to check chemical authenticity, supply-chain tracing, immediate suspension powers for imports linked to counterfeits or recalls, and new criminal penalties (up to 10 years imprisonment and a $250,000 fine) for online sellers of adulterated or counterfeit drugs or prescription-less dispensing. [S2]

It outlaws manufacturers charging certified foreign sellers more than local customers in the exporting country, restricting or delaying supplies to them, or making U.S.-market versions of a drug different from the exported version to defeat importation — the tactics drugmakers have used to keep cheaper imports from reaching Americans. [S2]

The bill directs enforcement discretion and waiver authority so individuals importing for personal use are not prosecuted or have shipments seized unless there is a significant public health threat. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, which lose the ability to segment markets and charge Americans far more than customers abroad for the same drugs. Insurance plans and employers, who today absorb part of high U.S. drug prices, could see pressure on negotiated prices as cheaper imported alternatives enter the supply chain.

drawbacks.text: If large volumes of U.S. demand are filled from limited supplies in Canada and smaller European markets, prices and availability in those exporting countries could be affected, which is why exporting countries have historically restricted bulk export of their drugs. [S2]

A multi-country importation program relies on certification, testing, and tracing by foreign sellers and FDA oversight; any gap in that system could let counterfeit or mishandled drugs reach patients, which is the safety concern import bans were originally justified on. The bill's suspension and testing provisions are designed for this but would depend on administration and funding. [S2]

The Secretary has broad discretion over certification criteria and could write regulations so restrictive that importation is legal in name only, as critics have argued happened with the limited 2003-era importation authority; the bill does not specify minimum quantities or timelines beyond the one-year rulemaking deadline. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is large: patients pay a fraction of U.S. prices for the same medicines, with safety protections built in. The real costs are borne by drugmakers' profits and are administrative on the public side — certifying sellers, testing, and tracing. The strongest honest objection is that safety depends entirely on how rigorously the FDA administers certification and testing, and that bulk importation could strain supply in smaller exporting markets. On balance the bill targets a well-documented price gap that costs Americans directly.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on June 26, 2024, received no hearing, markup, or floor vote, and died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced by Rep. Jan Schakowsky with 8 Democratic cosponsors on June 26, 2024. [S1][S3]
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, the committee with jurisdiction over drug law, and no further action was recorded. [S4]
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill expired without a vote; in the final two months of a Congress, unrefereed bills rarely advance. [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers keep the status quo: they continue selling the same medicines in the U.S. at several times the price charged in peer countries, with no competing imported supply. Patients who ration or skip medications continue to bear that cost.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers kept the status quo

for.name: Rep. Jan Schakowsky
for.role: Sponsor, introduced the bill in the House

for.name: Reps. Cohen, Doggett, Grijalva, Norton, Omar, Pingree, and Pocan
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction. [S2][S3]

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill after it was referred on June 26, 2024. [S4]

against.name: Pharmaceutical industry
against.what_they_did: The industry has long opposed importation legislation and lobbied against similar bills, arguing safety risks; no manufacturer supported this bill. [S2]

sides.party_line_note: All 9 supporters (the sponsor and 8 cosponsors) were House Democrats, and the Republican-controlled committee never took the bill up. [S3][S4]

industries.note: The bill would end their ability to charge Americans 2.78 times the average price in comparable countries for the same drugs by opening a legal import channel and outlawing price discrimination and supply restrictions against certified foreign sellers. Their loss is the direct source of patient savings, which is why their interest runs against the public's here. [S2]

industries.industry: U.S. pharmacies and wholesale drug distributors
industries.note: Registered U.S. pharmacies and wholesalers would become importers and could source qualifying drugs at lower foreign prices, potentially improving margins on dispensed prescriptions; they face new reporting, testing, and record-keeping obligations. [S2]

industries.industry: Certified foreign pharmacies and wholesalers (Canada, UK, EU, Switzerland)
industries.note: The bill creates a certified-seller regime with a public list and annual fees, giving compliant foreign pharmacies and distributors a new lawful U.S. customer base. Their access to U.S. demand is what delivers lower prices to patients. [S2]
